stories.title: AGIBOT shows a third-generation humanoid hardware platform and a new robot foundation model at its Innovation Day in Shanghai
paragraphs: Chinese humanoid robot maker AGIBOT held its AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026 in Shanghai on Oct. 29, 2026, according to the company's posts on X and a report by The Robot Report. AGIBOT introduced Worken, which it describes as a proposed framework for measuring the productive work robots do in real-world settings: the number of active robots, multiplied by their autonomous working hours, multiplied by an output efficiency ratio compared against a reference benchmark for the task.

The company also showed AHA3, its third-generation humanoid hardware architecture, which The Robot Report says adds a joint liquid-cooling system and IP67-rated joints for continuous industrial work. AGIBOT debuted GO-3 Preview, a next-generation robot foundation model built around what it calls a World Reasoning Action Model, and WITA-Omni 1.0, a model for human-robot interaction that combines vision, speech, real-time dialogue and movement.

AGIBOT launched G2 Max, an industrial robot with 21 degrees of freedom and a dual-arm handling capacity of up to 40 kg, and released Link-U OS 1.0, an operating system for embodied AI that it plans to make fully open source by the end of 2026, The Robot Report says. The outlet notes that AGIBOT said last month its 20,000th robot had rolled off the production line, and that IDC reported the company led global humanoid robot shipments in the first half of 2026. No prices or availability dates were given for the new hardware.

image.alt: AGIBOT president and CTO Peng Zhihui introduces Worken on stage at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026

stories.title: The White House finds robot and industrial machinery imports threaten U.S. national security and orders trade talks, with no tariffs for now
paragraphs: President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Oct. 28, 2026, agreeing with a Section 232 finding by the Secretary of Commerce that robotics, industrial machinery and their parts and components are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair U.S. national security, according to the text published by the White House. The proclamation says the United States relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery and their components, and that equipment from certain foreign entities can pose cybersecurity risks.

The proclamation specifically cites advanced robots, such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles, as providing combat support to the U.S. military, including reconnaissance, casualty extraction and mine clearing. It says robotics and industrial machinery supported about $7.1 trillion in shipments of manufactured goods in 2024 and the production of about $86 billion worth of equipment that year.

The order does not set tariffs. It directs the Commerce Secretary and the U.S. Trade Representative to negotiate agreements with trading partners and to report on progress within 180 days, and says the president may consider other remedies in the future, including tariffs, duties, quotas and fees, or a program to encourage new investment in U.S. production. The proclamation notes that Section 232 allows further action if an agreement is not reached within 180 days, is not carried out or is ineffective.

The Robot Report, which covered the decision on Oct. 29, quoted Boston Dynamics vice president of policy Brendan Schulman as saying the next step is negotiations over the next six months with trading partners. Ash Sharma of Interact Analysis told the outlet the move should not be read as a new robotics tariff today but shows the government's direction, and former Novanta robotics strategy chief Robert Little said his biggest concern is gaps in the U.S. supply of robot components such as sensors, actuators, precision gears and encoders.

image.credit: Office of the White House, via The Robot Report
image.alt: Image of the White House Section 232 proclamation on robotics imports

stories.title: North American robot orders jumped 24.8% in the third quarter of 2026, the strongest quarter of the year, A3 says
paragraphs: North American companies ordered 10,989 robots valued at $723.5 million in the third quarter of 2026, according to data from the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) reported by The Robot Report on Oct. 28, 2026. That is an increase of 24.8% in units and 26.1% in value compared with the third quarter of 2025, and A3 said it was the strongest quarter of the year so far. Orders for the first nine months of 2026 reached 28,984 robots worth about $1.89 billion, up 9.6% in units.

A3 said automotive OEM orders, which fell in the first half of the year, grew 7.5% in the third quarter, though they remain 17% below last year's level through September. Orders from automotive component suppliers rose 90.4%. Among other industries, A3 reported unit increases of 97.6% in semiconductors and electronics/photonics, 67.7% in plastics and rubber, 38.7% in life sciences, pharmaceutical and biomedical, and 37.0% in metals, while food and consumer goods orders fell 23.7%.

Collaborative robots, designed to work alongside people, also grew: companies ordered 1,831 of them worth $63.8 million in the quarter, about 56% more units than a year earlier, making up 16.7% of all robot units ordered, A3 said. "What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market," said Alex Shikany, executive vice president at A3.

A3 linked the growth in electronics to investment in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing and noted that higher input costs, trade uncertainty and the timing of large manufacturing projects remain factors to watch.

image.alt: A3 chart comparing robot orders by industry in the first nine months of 2026
